title: Love
lead: The central virtue of the New Testament, the Greek word agape (not to be confused with the early church meal also called agape): the love God has for people, the love believers are to have for God and for each other, and the love for enemies that Jesus taught. 1 Corinthians 13 is Paul's best-known description of it.

sections.b: The Old Testament commands love for God (Deuteronomy 6:5) and for one's neighbor (Leviticus 19:18), and describes the LORD as 'slow to anger, great in loyal love' (Exodus 34:6). Jesus names the two commands as the heart of the law (Matthew 22:37-40), and Paul says that love fulfills the law (Romans 13:8-10; Galatians 5:14).
sections.refs: Deuteronomy 6:5; Leviticus 19:18; Exodus 34:6; Matthew 22:37; Romans 13:8; Galatians 5:14

sections.b: Paul says that tongues, prophecy, knowledge, faith and giving away everything are nothing without love. He describes love by what it does: it is slow to anger, acts with kindness, is not jealous and does not show off, does not keep a record of wrongs, covers all things, trusts all things, hopes all things and holds firm through all things. It never collapses, though prophecy, tongues and knowledge will be set aside. 'The greatest of them is love.'

A popular teaching says agape is a special 'God-kind' of love, different from friendship (philia) and desire (eros). Scholars note that agape is a common word in the Greek Old Testament, where it can even mean Amnon's lust for Tamar (2 Samuel 13:15), and that in John 21:15-17 'love' (agape) and 'love' (philia) are used for the same thing. The Christian meaning comes from what Paul and the other writers fill the word with: the self-giving of Christ.
